subject: owl
reasoning:
I'm planning out the owl model: a roughly half-meter tall standing figure facing forward, with a skeleton starting from a pelvis root joint, plus wings, tail, legs, and a jointed beak for the rest pose.

Then I'm working out specific coordinates for the body ellipsoid, head sphere, neck, jaw hinge, and beak cones, followed by mirrored wing joints for each side.

For wing geometry, I'm weighing whether to build a chain of bones with extruded shapes or just represent the wing as a series of flattened boxes acting as primary feathers attached along the arm.

Building feather shapes...

Working out the cross product math to get the extrusion axes oriented correctly for each wing side...

For the wing layout, I'm planning feather placement: secondaries attaching along the forearm between elbow and wrist pointing mostly backward and outward, with primaries fanning from the wrist, all positioned in the x-z plane with the wing angled slightly downward.

Defining covert shapes...

Planning the flight feathers now: secondaries along the arm fanning backward, primaries from the wrist spreading outward with increasing length, using a helper function to generate each feather with position, direction, length, width, color, and bone attachment.

I'm mapping the skeleton joints — shoulder, elbow, wrist, finger — and deciding where coverts, secondaries, and primaries attach, plus assigning a color palette: brown and dark brown body tones, cream underparts, a pale face disk with a darker rim, and orange eyes.

For the body I'm compositing custom paint functions: a mottled back pattern blended with cream belly stripes, adjusting for the fact that an owl's belly faces forward rather than down, so I'm writing a normal-based paint function that switches pattern by surface direction.

Placing body parts next...

Working out disk placement and rotation so the facial discs sit flush against the head's curved surface, angled slightly outward to face forward.

I'll use a dir-based aiming helper instead of raw Euler angles — specifying a target direction and which local axis (Y for cylinders, Z for torus) should align with it. Now I'm figuring out the brow rotation sign so the inner ends slope downward toward the center on each side, then working out the beak geometry: a forward-and-down pointing cone for the upper beak, aimed using the same direction-based approach, with a smaller cone planned for the lower jaw.

Still placing the lower beak cone, then moving to ear tufts as small outward-tilted cones on the head bone. For the chest, I'm deciding to skip detailed feather cards and instead use horizontal cream-and-dark stripe patterns on the belly to suggest a bib.

Now I'm working out the tail: a joint angled back and down, with five fanned feathers extruded along that direction, and I'm deriving the math for the feather's normal vector using cross products so the fan orients correctly relative to the tail bone.

For color variety, I'm picking a two-tone brown scheme—darker primaries and a lighter mid-brown for secondaries—and setting up the extrude call parameters (thickness, bone binding) for each feather.

Now I'm moving to the legs: hip, knee, and ankle joints positioned down the body with a feathered cream-colored tarsus capsule, then working out zygodactyl toe placement with three forward and one back, spread at rest.

For the capsule bone weighting, I'll explicitly pass the bone name string so joints resolve correctly rather than relying on default point-based weighting. I'm also setting up a joint helper function that takes parent, position, aim direction, and role to simplify defining wing joints like the shoulder-to-chest connection.

For the tail, I'm considering using a chain of joints instead of individual joints, defining it as a polyline through several points with a parent of pelvis and role "tail" so it droops naturally downward and backward from the body, with feathers fanning out from the base.

I'm now working through legs similarly—deciding whether to use chains with role "leg" spanning hip, knee, and ankle, and figuring out how the names array should map to spans so the tip gets properly named for feather attachment.

Then I set up wing chains the same way—shoulder, elbow, wrist—with the tip named at the wrist, leaving finger digits for later and defaulting to standard chain-up behavior.

Working through the wing joint positions and coordinate math for the shoulder, elbow, wrist chain and the covert feather placement, figuring out directional vectors for the outline orientation...

I'll use the coat paint color for coverts, body, and head, setting thickness at 0.03 with wing coverts positioned around y=0.35 overlapping the arm area, parented to the shoulder bone before refining the elbow joint.

For the secondary feathers, I'm computing base positions along the arm using a loop parameter, placing each feather's root slightly trailing behind the wing with a backward-pointing direction vector, and checking that the feather width doesn't cause excessive overlap between neighboring quills given the spacing along the arm.

Now I'm setting up the primary feathers fanning out from the wrist, using an angle parameter sweeping from near-vertical to more outward to spread them across the wingtip, with the middle primaries being the longest to match an owl's natural wing shape and the outer ones tapering shorter.

Adjusting feather base positions to shift further outward and forward along the wing, checking the overall span totals roughly 1.2m which matches a realistic owl wingspan. I'm defining a simple convex feather outline shape for each barb, keeping it minimal without a rachis or tip detail for now.

Rather than painting individual stripes per feather since the texture chart count would get too high, I'll use alternating plain colors instead. I'm also setting up the ruff and facial disk rim details, then moving into the body's coat pattern using a mottled brown texture function for the back markings.

Still writing styles...

I'm checking the geometry so the eye disks sit proud of the head sphere's curved surface at every point, including near the edges, and nudging the yaw rotation slightly to angle them forward.

Now I'm placing the eyes as small spheres with pupils offset in front, positioned and scaled so they sit naturally on the face without needing extra highlight details, then setting the head sphere's scale to give it a slightly flattened shape.

For the beak, I'm positioning it between the eye disks and shaping the upper and lower cones so they angle downward and taper to a point.

I'm now adjusting pad spheres at the ankle and figuring out leg feather coverage down to the foot, then sketching the leg chain itself from hip to knee to ankle with thigh capsules sized appropriately.

I also want to add a few V-shaped chest feather markings and a tiny cream box between the eyes as a central facial strip.

Now I'm positioning a cream nose-bridge wedge near the head and defining joint coordinates for pelvis, chest, neck, head, and jaw, along with their aim directions for the spine chain and jaw. I'm setting bone parenting so wings attach to the chest and legs/tail attach to the pelvis, then moving into writing the actual feather-generation helper function using THREE.Vector3 math.
